title: Stress-scale error accounts for 29-34% of the recent NCEP heat-flux error change at 19 tropical buoy sites
abstract: We tested whether monthly stress-scale error can explain the recent NCEP latent heat-flux error change at 19 tropical buoy sites. An exact symmetric product split uses latent heat loss Q and A, the square root of monthly vector-stress length. It separates error in A from error in Q/A before averaging. For February 2023-December 2025 versus 2010-2019, total error changes are -19.86 W m-2 in R1 and -29.86 in R2. Stress-scale parts are -5.66 and -10.07, or 29% and 34% of the point totals. Ratio parts are -14.19 [-22.25, -6.31] and -19.78 [-28.45, -12.12], with conditional 95% block intervals. Alternate baselines, stress floors, exact joint-day buoy means and steady-direction checks retain negative ratio parts. The large ratio share is strongest in the Atlantic; Pacific R1 has a larger stress part. Two replacement orders give similar results. Independent scalar checks confirm closure and the main estimates. The ratio includes moisture difference, transfer physics and unresolved wind variability. It does not measure humidity or prove an SST cause. Sparse tropical coverage, bulk-flux error and shared observations limit inference. Code, source hashes, aggregate evidence and retrieval instructions are included.
